solution:
A charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) feels an electric force \(\vec{F}_e = q\vec{E}\) in an electric field and a magnetic force \(\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\) in a magnetic field. The two differ as follows.

| Electric force \(\vec{F}_e = q\vec{E}\) | Magnetic force \(\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\) |
|---|---|
| Acts on the charge whether it is at rest or moving. | Acts only on a MOVING charge. It is zero for a charge at rest, and zero when \(\vec{v}\) is parallel or antiparallel to \(\vec{B}\). |
| Its size \(qE\) does not depend on the velocity of the charge. | Its size \(qvB\sin\theta\) depends on the speed \(v\) and on the angle \(\theta\) between \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\). |
| It acts along \(\vec{E}\) (for a positive charge) or opposite to \(\vec{E}\) (for a negative charge). | It is always perpendicular to both \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\). |
| It can do work on the charge, so it can change the speed and the kinetic energy. | Being perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\), it does NO work. It changes only the direction of motion; the speed and kinetic energy stay constant. |
| A charge entering the field at an angle follows a parabola; a charge starting along the field moves in a straight line with uniform acceleration. | A charge entering perpendicular to the field moves in a circle; one entering at any other angle moves along a helix. |

When both fields are present, the total (Lorentz) force is \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})\).

**Condition.** A charged particle moves in a uniform circle when it enters a UNIFORM magnetic field with its velocity PERPENDICULAR to the field (and no other force acts). The magnetic force \(F = qvB\) is then always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of motion and supplies the centripetal force:

\(qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}\).

**Cyclotron: construction.** (The diagram shows the two dees seen from above, the gap between them, the source S at the centre, the spiral path of the ion, the oscillator joined across the dees and the deflector plate at the edge, with the field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to the dees.)
- Two hollow, semicircular metal boxes called dees, \(D_1\) and \(D_2\), are placed with a narrow gap between their straight edges.
- The dees are kept in a vacuum chamber between the poles of a strong electromagnet, which gives a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the dees.
- A high frequency oscillator is connected across the dees, so an alternating electric field acts across the gap. Inside a dee there is no electric field, because the metal shields it.
- A source S of positive ions is placed at the centre of the gap, and a deflector plate near the edge of one dee takes the ions out to the target.

**Working.** An ion from S is accelerated across the gap into the dee that is negative at that moment. Inside the dee it feels only the magnetic field, so it moves along a semicircle and comes back to the gap. By then the oscillator has reversed the polarity, so the ion is accelerated again into the other dee. At every crossing of the gap the ion gains energy, so its speed and the radius of its path \(r = mv/(qB)\) increase, and it moves out along a spiral. Near the edge the deflector plate draws it out as a high energy beam.

**Frequency of revolution.** The time to go round a semicircle is

\(t = \dfrac{\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{\pi m}{qB}\)

which does not depend on the speed or the radius. So the time period of one revolution is \(T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\), and the frequency of revolution (the cyclotron frequency) is

\(f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{qB}{2\pi m} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{q}{m}\right)B\)

where \(\dfrac{q}{m}\) is the specific charge of the ion. The oscillator frequency is set equal to this value (the resonance condition), so the ion always arrives at the gap when the field there is in the right direction to accelerate it.

**What is special about it.** In a radial magnetic field the lines of force are along the radii of a circle, like the spokes of a wheel. In a moving coil galvanometer it is produced by CONCAVE (cylindrical) pole pieces with a soft iron cylinder fixed inside the coil. Because of this:
- the plane of the coil always lies along the field lines, whatever the deflection of the coil, so the angle between the field and the normal to the coil is always \(90^\circ\);
- the field has the same magnitude \(B\) at every position of the sides of the coil.

**Why it is useful.** The torque on a coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) carrying current \(I\) is \(\tau = NIAB\sin\theta\). In a radial field \(\theta = 90^\circ\) for every position, so

\(\tau = NIAB\)

which stays the same for all deflections. The coil turns until this torque is balanced by the restoring torque of the suspension, \(c\phi\), where \(c\) is the torsion constant and \(\phi\) the deflection:

\(NIAB = c\phi\), so \(I = \left(\dfrac{c}{NAB}\right)\phi\), that is, \(I \propto \phi\).

So the deflection is directly proportional to the current, and the galvanometer can have a UNIFORM (linear) scale. The soft iron core also makes the field stronger, which increases the sensitivity of the galvanometer.

[Textbook misprint: the book prints "Biot-Savert". The law is the Biot-Savart law, named after Jean-Baptiste Biot and Felix Savart, and the book's own Chapter 10 text spells it correctly. The question is preserved as printed and is unaffected.]

**Biot-Savart law.** The magnetic field \(dB\) produced at a point P by a small current element \(I\,dl\) is
- directly proportional to the current \(I\) and to the length \(dl\) of the element,
- directly proportional to \(\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(d\vec{l}\) and the position vector \(\vec{r}\) of P from the element,
- inversely proportional to the square of the distance \(r\).

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}\), or in vector form \(d\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \vec{r}}{r^3}\)

where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m/A. The direction of \(d\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to the plane containing \(d\vec{l}\) and \(\vec{r}\).

**(i) Infinitely long straight conductor.** Let the wire carry current \(I\), and let P be at perpendicular distance \(a\) from it, with O the foot of the perpendicular. Take an element \(dl\) at distance \(l\) from O. If \(\phi\) is the angle between \(\vec{r}\) and OP, then

\(l = a\tan\phi\), so \(dl = a\sec^2\phi\,d\phi\); \(r = a\sec\phi\); and \(\sin\theta = \cos\phi\).

Every element gives a field at P in the same direction (perpendicular to the plane of the wire and P), so the fields simply add:

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{a\sec^2\phi\,d\phi\,\cos\phi}{a^2\sec^2\phi} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\cos\phi\,d\phi\)

For an infinitely long wire \(\phi\) runs from \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) to \(+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\):

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\phi\,d\phi = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi a}(2) = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi a}\)

The field lines are circles around the wire, in the sense given by the right hand rule.

**(ii) Point on the axis of a circular loop.** Let the loop have radius \(R\) and current \(I\), and let P be on its axis at distance \(z\) from the centre. For every element \(d\vec{l}\), the vector \(\vec{r}\) to P is perpendicular to \(d\vec{l}\), and \(r^2 = R^2 + z^2\). So

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2 + z^2}\)

\(d\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{r}\). Resolve it along the axis and perpendicular to the axis. For the element at the opposite end of a diameter the perpendicular components are equal and opposite, so they cancel over the whole loop. The axial components all point the same way and add. If \(\alpha\) is the angle between \(\vec{r}\) and the axis, the axial component is \(dB\sin\alpha\), with \(\sin\alpha = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{R^2 + z^2}}\):

\(B = \displaystyle\oint \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\,\dfrac{I\,dl}{R^2 + z^2}\cdot\dfrac{R}{(R^2 + z^2)^{1/2}} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R}{4\pi (R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\,(2\pi R)\)

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\), directed along the axis.

For a coil of \(N\) turns, \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\). At the centre \((z = 0)\) this becomes \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\), and far away \((z \gg R)\) it becomes \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2z^3}\).

**Ampere's law.** The line integral of the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) around any closed path (an Amperian loop) is equal to \(\mu_0\) times the net current enclosed by that path:

\(\displaystyle\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I\)

The sign of each current is fixed by the right hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along the direction in which the loop is traversed; a current along the stretched thumb is positive and one opposite to it is negative. Currents outside the loop do not count.

**How it is useful.** Ampere's law holds for every closed path, but it is useful for finding \(B\) when the current has symmetry. Then we choose a loop on which \(B\) has the same magnitude everywhere and is either along \(d\vec{l}\) or perpendicular to it. The integral becomes simple and \(B\) can be found directly, without the long integration of the Biot-Savart law. It plays the same role for magnetic fields that Gauss's law plays in electrostatics.

- **Long straight wire.** Take a circle of radius \(r\) around the wire. \(B\) is the same all round and along the circle: \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\), so \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\).
- **Inside a long straight wire of radius \(a\)** carrying a uniform current \(I\). A circle of radius \(r < a\) encloses the current \(I\dfrac{r^2}{a^2}\): \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\dfrac{r^2}{a^2}\), so \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi a^2}\), which grows linearly with \(r\).
- **Long solenoid** with \(n\) turns per unit length. Take a rectangular loop with one side of length \(L\) inside the solenoid, parallel to its axis. Only that side contributes (outside \(B \approx 0\), and on the two ends \(\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(d\vec{l}\)): \(BL = \mu_0 nLI\), so \(B = \mu_0 nI\) inside, uniform along the length.
- **Toroid** with \(N\) turns. Take a circle of radius \(r\) inside the core: \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 NI\), so \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 NI}{2\pi r}\). For a circle in the open space inside the toroid, or outside it, the net enclosed current is zero, so \(B = 0\) there.

Ampere's law in this form applies to steady currents.
